scenes.title: How do you graph y = 2x + 1?
body: How do you know the next point?
scenes.narration: Suppose you need to graph y equals two x plus one. Where should your first point go, and how do you know where the line goes next? Here’s the idea: a linear equation gives you both a starting value and a constant rate of change.

scenes.title: The intercept is the starting value
scenes.narration: In y equals m x plus b, b is the y-intercept. It tells you the value of y when x is zero, so b equals one means the graph starts at zero comma one. This is where students often mix things up: the y-intercept is not one comma zero. It lies on the y-axis, and every point on the y-axis has x equal to zero.

scenes.title: Slope tells you the movement
scenes.narration: Now look at the slope. m equals two, which we can write as two over one. The numerator is the change in y, and the denominator is the change in x. So from zero comma one, move right one and up two to reach one comma three. Notice why rise goes over run: slope measures vertical change for each unit of horizontal change. Reversing those gives a different rate.

scenes.title: A line repeats the same rate
body: Each step: +1 in x, +2 in y
scenes.narration: Repeat the same movement: right one, up two, and you reach two comma five. Because a linear function has a constant rate of change, that same rise-over-run pattern keeps producing points on one straight line. We can check the point two comma five in the equation: two times two plus one equals five, so the graph and equation agree.

scenes.title: Read the equation before drawing
body: m = change in y per change in x
scenes.narration: So graphing a linear function is not about memorizing a drawing trick. The intercept tells you where the line starts when x is zero, and the slope tells you how the output changes as the input changes. Plot the starting point, repeat the rate to get another reliable point, then draw the line through them. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
